title: Many open number-theory problems may be unprovable from arithmetic's axioms

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Many open number-theory problems may be unprovable from arithmetic's axioms

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A fair fraction of the unsolved problems seriously studied in number theory will turn out to be questions that cannot be answered using the standard axioms of arithmetic.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And it is my strong suspicion that in fact of all the current unsolved problems seriously studied in number theory a fair fraction will in the end turn out to be questions that cannot ever be answered using the normal axioms of arithmetic.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Implications for Mathematics and Its Foundations” (from p. 772), p. 791. Scope: open problems in number theory relative to Peano arithmetic

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-36: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.42

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing problem catalogs can define a sample but do not contain the independence proofs needed for resolution. The necessary mathematical results would be major new knowledge, and the vague prevalence threshold further lowers operationalizability.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Create a dated census of seriously studied open number-theory statements formalized in a fixed arithmetic theory, then prove independence or derivability for each and compute the independent fraction. A low fraction refutes, and a prespecified substantial fraction confirms, the prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Most independence results are unknown.

"Fair fraction" and "seriously studied" are unspecified.

The denominator changes over time and with problem formulation.

fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.3

data existence: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.6

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Once a list is fixed, each problem is independent of arithmetic or it is not, so the sentence is not empty. Public mathematics contains independence proofs for carefully built statements, and it does not decide the open problems number theorists study. Computation and observation do not generate those independence proofs, so the predicted fraction cannot be resolved with resources that exist now.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fix a list of unsolved problems studied in number theory and determine what fraction are independent of the usual axioms of arithmetic. Each problem is independent or it is not; producing those independence results is a family of proofs, and computation of special cases does not yield them.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Independence of a specific arithmetic statement is not produced by computation or by the absence of a known proof.

A fair fraction and seriously studied require a closed list the claim does not give.

A proof in a stronger theory leaves open whether arithmetic alone sufficed.
